content.text: Gammons: Former Tiger Willie Horton on Detroit, progress, division and respect By Peter Gammons Jun 13, 2020 36 Last Thursday afternoon, Willie Horton was working in his yard in the Detroit suburb of Bloomfield Hills. Indoors, his wife, Gloria, watched the George Floyd service. Willie occasionally came in and intently watched, repeating the words, “we are blessed.” He talked on the phone about their many grandchildren and great-grandchildren, and, as he has done all 77 years of his life, expressed optimism. “The progress that is being made in Detroit some days brings tears to my eyes,” he said. “But what’s going on around our country is at the point where we have to have the leadership to get together and make changes, or this is going to be difficult to overcome.” Willie Horton has a street named for him. He is one of four native Detroiters to have a day named for him; Rosa Parks is the third. On his childhood paper route, what is now Comerica Park was on the route, and there was a wall where he stopped and played a game called “strike the wall.” He was raised in housing projects. As a young player in the Tigers’ Lakeland spring training camp, he had to drink from the “colored” fountain, not the same one as white players. On July 23, 1967, when violence broke out near his old 12th Street neighborhood, after a game with the Yankees at Tiger Stadium, he got in his car, drove down to what he describes “a war” and, in his uniform, tried to calm the violence. He worked for Mayor Coleman Young in his youth, and when Mike Ilitch, a Coleman confidant bought the team, they united their lifetime love of their city. In a normal season, Gloria and Willie live in their Polk County, Fla., home and oversee Horton 360 — a program dedicated to help kids, schools, seniors and veterans in the area in central Florida – then return home to Detroit for the remainder of the year. For most of his baseball life, Horton has been a man other players turned to in times of need, from a young Tiger outfielder in the Sixties named Art James to Blue Moon Odom and Vida Blue. Al Kaline once called Willie Horton “a man among men.” Horton looks back at those 1967 riots, and the violence that broke out after the Tigers finished beating the Padres in the fifth and final game of the 1984 World Series. He remembers that 21 months before that final game and the unrest, Detroit’s signature downtown department store, Hudson’s, had closed down. “I look back on where we were then, and where we’ve come,” says Horton. “Hudson’s is going to be re-opening in 2022. The area near there is being brought back. People are moving back. I am so proud of the young people coming into Detroit. It can be done.” In 1950, before Horton and his family moved to Detroit, the population was 1.86 million. The 2020 listing is around 667,000. But other demographics are pointing upwards. “It’s black and white, young and old, respect. Respect. That’s what I loved so much about playing baseball, with Al Kaline, Eddie Mathews, Earl Wilson, Mickey Stanley, Mickey Lolich. We went out and got Mathews and John Wyatt and Earl Wilson and they were really important to winning that World Series in 1968. “But what I see now is a country dangerously divided. When I was a teenager, my parents had my sister and I live with a man who really helped our family, a judge named Damon Keith. He had a tremendous impact on my life. His values helped us raising seven kids. We had two boys who helped raise their sisters, making sure they did the right things. Two of my boys became ministers, who devote their lives to helping people. “But it’s dangerous,” says Horton, “to see such division. I learned from my granddaddy that it’s not about black and white, it’s about people. It shouldn’t be about politics, it should be about people. If we don’t figure this out and come together, I’m very worried for the future.” Willie Horton grew up in the Detroit projects when deindustrialization and unemployment ate at the city. He had to walk to the park in Lakeland because cab drivers didn’t drive African Americans. He stood in his uniform in July of 1967 in the chaos and pleaded for peace. He and Gloria have been married for 59 years, have 45 grandchildren and greatgrandchildren, and people of all backgrounds still call him because he is a healer. He understands all of Marvin Gaye’s emotions when he sang “Inner City Blues,” because Willie was there, and Marvin Gaye was his longtime neighbor and friend in Bloomfield Hills. As he watched the George Floyd memorial last week, within a half-dozen sentences he said “I always believe that we can learn and bounce back,” paused, and added, “but if we get it wrong, I’m very worried about where we go.” (Top photo of Horton in 2016: Dave Reginek /
A Wonderful Tribute! Blessings!🙏🏾 Pastor Gainous
